newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine workers stage 36-hour general strike.
newsitem.headline: Argentine workers stage 36-hour general strike.

text.p: Argentine labour unions, pinched by austerity measures and shaken by high unemployment, launched a 36-hour general strike on Thursday in their biggest challenge yet to President Carlos Menem's free-market reforms.

The strike by the CGT, the largest labour federation, which has traditionally backed the ruling Peronists, highlighted growing discontent with recent tax increases, cuts to worker benefits, labour reforms and joblessness.

The walkout that began at noon (1500 GMT) had a moderate early impact as hospitals provided only emergency care, some flights were delayed or cancelled and garbage collection stopped. Traffic thinned and financial markets had what one trader called "a wasted day" of slow business.
But the worst was expected after 8 p.m. when buses, commuter trains and subway workers were set to walk out.

A defiant President Carlos Menem vowed to continue with reforms which, while slashing annual inflation to zero from 5,000 percent when he took office in 1989, have more than doubled unemployment to its current 17.1 percent.
"Strikes don't stop laws," Menem wrote in a letter in La Nacion newspaper on Thursday, suggesting workers who walked out were only interested in enjoying a long weekend.

The CGT was planning a rally in the Plaza de Mayo outside government house, bringing to Menem's front door discontent that has pushed his support in opinion polls to just 14-20 percent, compared with 50 percent in May 1995's re-election.
"Menem's margin to continue with policies that have produced monstrous unemployment, recession and social discontent is narrowing," opposition Radical Party leader Rodolfo Terragno said.

Menem's planned reforms are designed to lower employers' costs and give them flexibility to change working conditions to suit the economic climate, making them more competitive. It would loosen rules on working hours and holidays, allow for wages to vary depending on business conditions, scrap collective wage bargaining and replace unemployment pay with insurance schemes funded by employers.
The government predicts that employers, with lower costs, will hire workers again and help slash the jobless rate to single digit levels by the end of the decade.

Congress approved late on Wednesday a belt-tightening package to narrow the budget deficit that includes an increase in fuel taxes. It is also set to approve a law slapping taxes on widely used food vouchers and eliminating family allowance benefits for workers earning more than $1,500 a month.

Many Argentines plunged their largest cities into darkness this month in a five minute "blackout" organised by the opposition to protest austerity measures. They turned out the lights, banged pots and pans and honked their car horns.
